questions.text: A colleague asks what confidentiality means in practice. Which example fits best?

options.text: Only people with a legitimate need can view the information.
A file is copied to several personal devices.
Every change is recorded, whether authorized or not.
The information is always available, even during an outage.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality is about preventing unauthorized viewing or disclosure.

questions.text: A ransomware incident prevents staff opening important files. Which security goal is most directly affected?

options.text: Identity verification
Confidentiality only
Availability
Data minimization

questions.explanation: Availability means authorized people can use systems and information when work requires them.

questions.text: An employee receives a fake supplier invoice. What is the fake invoice message in the threat-weakness-risk example?

options.text: The approved control
The business impact
The vulnerability
The threat

questions.explanation: The message is the threat; skipping normal payment checks is the weakness, and misdirected payment is the risk.

questions.text: You receive an MFA prompt but are not signing in. What should you do?

options.text: Approve it so the notification goes away.
Deny it and report it through the approved channel.
Ignore repeated prompts and continue working.
Send the code to a colleague to check it.

questions.explanation: An unexpected prompt may mean someone has your password. Do not approve it; report it.

questions.text: A spreadsheet contains customer details for an external partner. What is the safest way to share it?

options.text: Copy every customer field in case it becomes useful.
Confirm the recipient, use the approved sharing method and include only needed details.
Share a public link and ask the partner not to forward it.
Send it to the partner's personal email for convenience.

questions.explanation: Verify who needs the information, limit it to what is necessary, and use approved tools.

questions.text: You step away from a laptop in a shared meeting room for a short call. What should you do first?

options.text: Leave it open because you will be back soon.
Ask a visitor to watch it.
Lock the screen.
Turn off endpoint protection to save battery.

questions.explanation: A brief absence is enough for someone to access an unattended session; lock the screen.

questions.text: A work browser starts behaving strangely after you opened an unexpected link. What is the best response?

options.text: Delete browser history and wait to see if it happens again.
Install a cleanup tool from a search result.
Follow incident instructions and contact IT or security promptly.
Forward the link to coworkers to ask if it is safe.

questions.explanation: Report promptly and follow the organization's process; avoid unapproved investigation or fixes.

questions.text: Why should employees use only the access needed for their current role?

options.text: It means access reviews are no longer needed.
It limits what could be exposed or changed if an account is misused.
It guarantees that phishing emails will be blocked.
It makes shared passwords easier to remember.

questions.explanation: Least privilege reduces unnecessary access and limits potential impact.

questions.text: What is the safest approach to software updates on a managed work device?

options.text: Use an update file from any website that looks official.
Install them through the organization's approved process.
Disable updates if a notification is inconvenient.
Ask a friend to install a modified version.

questions.explanation: Updates should come through approved channels; don't bypass organizational controls.

questions.text: You sent a work file to the wrong recipient. You are unsure whether they opened it. What should you do?

options.text: Report it promptly and explain what was sent and to whom.
Wait until you can prove information was accessed.
Hide the email and hope the recipient deletes it.
Contact the recipient privately before telling anyone.

questions.explanation: A suspected mistake is reportable; early, honest reporting lets the organization assess and limit exposure.

questions.text: A team member says a system is secure as long as outsiders cannot read its files. Which other goals belong with confidentiality?

options.text: Identity and authorization
Backups and encryption
Integrity and availability
Privacy and convenience

questions.explanation: The CIA triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability.

questions.text: A record is changed without approval and now shows the wrong payment amount. Which goal has been harmed?

options.text: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication

questions.explanation: Integrity is about information remaining accurate and being changed appropriately.

questions.text: An attacker exploits an employee skipping the normal bank-detail verification. In this example, what is the skipped check?

options.text: A security objective
The resulting financial loss
The threat actor
A vulnerability or weakness

questions.explanation: The missed process is a weakness that a threat can exploit; the risk is a wrong payment.

questions.text: A notification asks you to approve a work sign-in you did not start. Which action is safest?

options.text: Share the code so IT can investigate.
Reply to the notification asking who sent it.
Reject the request and tell IT/security using a known route.
Approve it once, then change your password later.

questions.explanation: Only approve authentication you initiated. Use a known reporting channel.

questions.text: Before sending a file with staff information, what should you check?

options.text: Whether the recipient can forward the attachment.
Whether the file name sounds generic.
Whether your personal cloud has more storage.
Whether the recipient is authorized and needs the information.

questions.explanation: Check the need, recipient and approved sharing method; remove unnecessary fields.

questions.text: You leave a signed-in workstation at a hot desk while getting coffee. What small action reduces risk?

options.text: Turn the monitor off only.
Close the browser but leave the session unlocked.
Lock the screen before leaving.
Write your password near the keyboard.

questions.explanation: Locking prevents someone nearby from using the open session.

questions.text: You accidentally opened a suspicious attachment and notice unusual device behavior. What information should you provide when reporting?

options.text: Nothing until you have completed your own investigation.
A copy forwarded to the whole department.
What happened, when, which device/account, and what you did.
Only your guess about who attacked you.

questions.explanation: The response team needs clear facts and actions taken, not speculative investigation.

questions.text: A contractor asks for administrator access even though they only need to view one report. What is the best response?

options.text: Grant broad access to avoid delays.
Share your own login temporarily.
Email the report to a personal account.
Use the normal approval process to grant only the necessary access.

questions.explanation: Access should match the task and be approved; accounts should not be shared.

questions.text: A pop-up offers an update for a work app from an unfamiliar download site. What should you do?

options.text: Install it if the logo looks familiar.
Ask a coworker to copy their installed files.
Disable security software so installation succeeds.
Use the organization's approved update process or ask IT.

questions.explanation: Unapproved downloads can introduce malware; follow managed update procedures.

questions.text: You find an unexpected USB drive labelled with your department's name. What is safest?

options.text: Do not plug it in; report or hand it over using the approved process.
Use it only if no files appear at first.
Open it on a work laptop to identify its owner.
Take it home to scan it privately.

questions.explanation: Unknown removable media can carry malware or expose information.

questions.text: A colleague says security is only an IT team's job. Which reply best reflects the module?

options.text: Security matters only when a breach is confirmed.
Employees should never report issues directly.
Only technical staff can reduce cyber risk.
Everyone's everyday choices help protect people, information and systems.

questions.explanation: Cybersecurity is shared responsibility; employees should use safer habits and report concerns.

questions.text: A file is accurate but unavailable to staff who need it during work. Which part of the CIA triad is affected?

options.text: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Least privilege

questions.explanation: Availability concerns timely access for authorized users.

questions.text: An unexpected request asks you to bypass the usual payment process. What does the module recommend?

options.text: Reply to the same email asking for confirmation.
Pay first and report later.
Pause and verify through a trusted channel before acting.
Treat the urgency as proof it is genuine.

questions.explanation: Unexpected or urgent requests should be checked using a separate trusted route.

questions.text: You notice an application has access to information unrelated to your job. What should you do?

options.text: Raise it with the appropriate support or security team.
Ignore it because access was granted by a system.
Share the access with your team.
Open more files to see what else you can access.

questions.explanation: Excessive or unnecessary permissions should be reported, not tested.

questions.text: A coworker needs a business document. Which sharing choice best protects it?

options.text: Send it to a personal email address.
Post it on a public link with a difficult-to-guess name.
Copy it into a public AI tool for convenience.
Use an approved tool and give access only to the intended recipient.

questions.explanation: Approved storage and recipient-limited sharing reduce accidental exposure.

questions.text: Your laptop is secured by a password, but it is missing after travel. What should you do?

options.text: Report it immediately and follow support instructions.
Try to track it using an unapproved app.
Wait a day in case it turns up.
Assume the password makes reporting unnecessary.

questions.explanation: A missing device must be reported promptly even if protected; the organization can protect accounts and data.

questions.text: A colleague says not to report a suspicious login until they know it was a real attack. What is the better approach?

options.text: Report the alert promptly; certainty is not required.
Post a screenshot publicly for advice.
Delete the alert to avoid confusion.
Wait for financial loss to occur.

questions.explanation: Employees should report concerns even if they are unsure; responders can assess them.

questions.text: Why should you avoid putting sensitive work details in a personal account?

options.text: Personal accounts always delete files immediately.
It makes MFA impossible to use.
The account or service may not be approved to protect that information.
It prevents authorized colleagues from seeing any information.

questions.explanation: Use approved tools because personal services may not meet organizational handling requirements.

questions.text: A security tool blocks a file you need for work. What should you do?

options.text: Download another copy from an unknown site.
Ask IT for guidance instead of disabling the tool.
Ask a coworker to send it through a private chat.
Turn off protection and reopen the file.

questions.explanation: Do not bypass security controls; use the support process.

questions.text: What is the best reason to report a mistake quickly, even if it feels embarrassing?

options.text: Early reporting can help limit harm and restore normal work sooner.
It automatically proves who caused the problem.
It removes the need to follow incident instructions.
It guarantees no one will ask questions.

questions.explanation: Timely reporting gives responders a better chance to contain and recover from an incident.

questions.text: A message uses your manager's name and asks for gift cards urgently. What should you do?

options.text: Buy the cards and send the codes quickly.
Trust it because the display name is familiar.
Call the manager using a number already in your directory.
Reply to the email asking if it is real.

questions.explanation: Verify an unusual payment request using a separate, previously trusted contact route.

questions.text: A text says your work account will close unless you sign in through its link. Which response is safest?

options.text: Open the link but do not type your password.
Enter your password to prevent account closure.
Avoid the link and use your normal sign-in route or contact IT.
Forward the text to a coworker and ask them to try it.

questions.explanation: Unexpected links may lead to fake sign-in pages; navigate using a known route.

questions.text: A caller claiming to be IT asks for your one-time MFA code. What is the safest response?

options.text: Read it out if the caller knows your name.
Send it by chat after the call.
Do not share it; contact the help desk independently.
Approve the prompt to test the caller.

questions.explanation: Passwords and one-time codes should never be shared with someone who contacts you.

questions.text: A supplier emails new bank details just before an invoice is due. What should happen before payment?

options.text: Use the number in the email signature.
Reply to the email asking for a second confirmation.
Change the details immediately to avoid a late fee.
Call a previously verified supplier number and follow approval steps.

questions.explanation: Payment changes should never be verified by email alone; use known contact details.

questions.text: Which clue should make you slow down and check a message?

options.text: It pressures you to act immediately or keep the request secret.
It comes through the normal approved workflow.
It matches a task you expected and was confirmed separately.
It uses the organization's usual reporting address.

questions.explanation: Urgency, authority and secrecy are common pressure tactics, especially around money or credentials.

questions.text: A phishing email is written specifically for one employee and refers to their current project. What is this targeted approach often called?

options.text: A verified internal announcement
A routine software update
Spear phishing
A password manager alert

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is tailored to a particular person, team or organization.

questions.text: You opened an unexpected attachment and then the computer behaves oddly. What should you do?

options.text: Download a repair utility from the web.
Delete the attachment and say nothing.
Report it promptly and follow the response team's instructions.
Send the file to coworkers to see if theirs opens.

questions.explanation: Report both the action and observed behavior; follow the organization's incident process.

questions.text: A QR code on a work poster asks you to log into a service. What should you check?

options.text: Whether other people have scanned it.
Whether the sign includes a familiar logo.
Whether the QR code is printed neatly.
Whether the request is expected and the destination is an approved, genuine site.

questions.explanation: QR codes can conceal destinations; verify the URL and use normal trusted routes.

questions.text: An email asks you to enable macros to view an invoice you were not expecting. What is safest?

options.text: Do not enable them; verify the file with the sender through a trusted route.
Open the file on a personal computer.
Turn off endpoint protection first.
Enable them if the invoice looks professional.

questions.explanation: Unexpected files and requests to enable unsafe features should be treated cautiously.

questions.text: You clicked a suspicious link but closed it without entering details. What should you do?

options.text: Clear browser history and keep quiet.
Report the click and follow guidance; be honest about what happened.
Assume there is no risk because you did not type a password.
Wait until you see a charge on your account.

questions.explanation: Even a click may matter; prompt reporting helps the team decide what checks are needed.

questions.text: A message from an apparent director says the request is confidential and must be completed in ten minutes. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Forward it to a large group for a quick vote.
Treat seniority as permission to skip checks.
Pause and verify via a known contact method while following normal approvals.
Send credentials because the message is confidential.

questions.explanation: Authority and urgency are pressure tactics; normal approval checks still apply.

questions.text: Which method is strongest for confirming an unexpected payment change?

options.text: Click the phone number in the message.
Check whether the email has a company logo.
Reply to the sender from the same thread.
Call the supplier using a number from trusted records.

questions.explanation: Use a separate, previously verified communication route.

questions.text: A fake login page looks exactly like the real one. Which detail can help expose it?

options.text: The page's color scheme alone.
The sender's display name alone.
The actual web address and whether you reached it through a trusted route.
The presence of a padlock icon alone.

questions.explanation: Visual design and display names can be copied; inspect the domain and navigate directly.

questions.text: A teammate wants to send you an authentication code because a caller says they are support. What should you tell them?

options.text: Send it if the caller sounds calm.
Never share a one-time code; verify the caller independently.
Use the code to see whether the caller can sign in.
Share it only if the caller knows your employee number.

questions.explanation: A code is an authentication secret and should not be disclosed to callers or chat contacts.

questions.text: An email appears to come from a real supplier and continues an existing thread, but requests a bank-account change. What should you remember?

options.text: Only new email addresses can be fraudulent.
Payment details can be changed without approval if the invoice is due.
A real mailbox or thread may be compromised, so verify the change independently.
An existing thread proves the request is safe.

questions.explanation: Business email compromise can use a compromised mailbox and existing conversation.

questions.text: A link-shortened message says you won a work prize and must claim it now. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Enter work credentials to confirm eligibility.
Open it quickly before the offer expires.
Do not rush; inspect through a trusted route or report it.
Share it with coworkers so they can check first.

questions.explanation: Urgent unexpected links should not be followed blindly; report uncertainty.

questions.text: You are unsure whether an email is phishing, but nothing has happened yet. Should you report it?

options.text: Only if a coworker agrees it is suspicious.
Wait until the sender requests money.
No, only confirmed attacks count.
Yes, use the approved reporting method even when uncertain.

questions.explanation: The reporting process is there for uncertain suspicious messages too.

questions.text: A message says to call a number included in it to verify a password reset. Which choice is safer?

options.text: Reply with your password and ask for help.
Search for a random support number online and share your details.
Use the organization's directory or support number you already trust.
Call the number in the message.

questions.explanation: Do not use contact details supplied by a suspicious message; use known information.

questions.text: A QR code is placed over a legitimate-looking event notice. What should you do before scanning or signing in?

options.text: Scan it with a personal phone to avoid work controls.
Check the destination and confirm the event or request through a trusted source.
Assume it is safe because the paper notice is official-looking.
Enter credentials if the page uses the right colors.

questions.explanation: QR codes can hide malicious URLs; verify the destination and expected context.

questions.text: You opened an attachment and later realize it was suspicious. What information is most useful in your report?

options.text: When it arrived, what you opened, what happened afterward and any steps you took.
A statement that you did nothing, even if you clicked it.
Only a guess about the attacker's identity.
A forwarded attachment sent to the whole office.

questions.explanation: Accurate reporting helps responders triage and respond; don't hide a mistake.

questions.text: A colleague receives a request from a 'CEO' to transfer funds and not tell finance. What warning signs are present?

options.text: Only a harmless writing mistake.
An approved routine payment process.
A verified change communicated by the supplier's known contact.
Urgency, authority and an attempt to bypass normal controls.

questions.explanation: Scammers commonly exploit authority, secrecy and pressure to bypass checks.

questions.text: A message asks you to sign in using a link, but you cannot tell whether the domain is genuine. What should you do?

options.text: Trust it if HTTPS appears.
Try it in a private browser window.
Do not use it; navigate through your normal bookmark or ask IT.
Enter only your username to test it.

questions.explanation: Use known addresses and remember HTTPS alone does not establish legitimacy.

questions.text: Someone on the phone says they need your MFA code to stop an attack. What is the safe response?

options.text: Share it because the caller says it is an emergency.
Refuse to share it and call the help desk using known contact details.
Send it only after the caller confirms your manager's name.
Read it aloud but change your password later.

questions.explanation: Do not share one-time codes; independently verify the caller.

questions.text: A new bank account appears in an emailed supplier invoice. What should you do before changing records?

options.text: Accept it if the sender's name matches the supplier.
Confirm the change with the supplier using a known number and follow approvals.
Use the email reply address to request confirmation.
Pay a small amount first to see if it arrives.

questions.explanation: Email can be compromised or spoofed; payment changes require separate verification.

questions.text: Which combination makes a suspicious message more concerning?

options.text: A message that contains no links or action request.
Unexpected request plus pressure to share credentials or money.
Expected routine notice through an approved system.
Known sender and independently confirmed request.

questions.explanation: Unexpectedness and sensitive actions are cues to pause, verify and report.

questions.text: A fake message uses correct grammar and your organization's branding. Is that enough to trust it?

options.text: Yes, because scammers usually make spelling errors.
Yes, if it arrived during business hours.
Yes, if the logo is current.
No; check the sender, destination and context independently.

questions.explanation: Modern phishing can be polished; no single appearance cue proves legitimacy.

questions.text: After clicking a suspicious link, you did not enter details. What is the best next move?

options.text: Report what happened promptly and follow the organization's advice.
Keep browsing unless a warning appears.
Delete the message and avoid mentioning the click.
Send the link to your personal email for analysis.

questions.explanation: Report the event accurately so the response team can assess it.

questions.text: A file from an unexpected sender asks you to enable macros. What should you do?

options.text: Disable antivirus before viewing it.
Enable them if the sender's name is familiar.
Copy the file to a USB drive and open it elsewhere.
Do not enable them; verify the request using a trusted channel.

questions.explanation: Unexpected attachments and requests to enable active content can be dangerous.

questions.text: A supplier's email address or display name has been altered to look genuine. What is this tactic called?

options.text: Account recovery
Data minimization
Least privilege
Spoofing

questions.explanation: Spoofing makes a sender, phone number or website appear to belong to someone else.

questions.text: You suspect a phishing message but have not replied or clicked. What should you do?

options.text: Post the message publicly to warn everyone.
Delete it and assume coworkers are protected.
Report it through the organization's approved channel.
Reply to ask the sender to prove their identity.

questions.explanation: Use the official reporting method; avoid interacting with or broadly forwarding it.

questions.text: Why should important accounts have unique passwords?

options.text: Unique passwords remove the need for MFA.
A breach of one service is less likely to expose other accounts.
They make shared accounts easier to manage.
They guarantee every sign-in is genuine.

questions.explanation: Reusing a password lets attackers try the same credential elsewhere.

questions.text: You receive repeated MFA prompts while not signing in. What should you do?

options.text: Approve one to stop the alerts.
Send a code to the caller who asks first.
Turn off MFA for the account.
Deny them and contact IT/security through a known channel.

questions.explanation: Repeated unexpected prompts may indicate someone has your password; reject and report them.

questions.text: A coworker cannot open a shared folder and asks to borrow your login. What is the safest response?

options.text: Do not share your account; help them request their own access.
Give them your password for the day.
Approve their access while they use your session.
Write your code on a note for them.

questions.explanation: Shared logins weaken accountability; each person should use their own approved access.

questions.text: Where should you store work passwords if your organization provides a password manager?

options.text: In the approved password manager.
In a note app that is not approved.
In a shared spreadsheet for the team.
In a personal email draft.

questions.explanation: Use only approved password storage; personal notes or shared files can expose credentials.

questions.text: A sign-in alert shows an unfamiliar device. What should you do?

options.text: Click any link in an alert email to investigate.
Ignore it if you can still access the account.
Report it using the organization's known route and follow recovery guidance.
Ask coworkers to try logging in as you.

questions.explanation: Report unfamiliar sign-ins through trusted organizational channels, not links in unexpected emails.

questions.text: You reused a personal password for work and hear that the personal service was breached. What is the best next step?

options.text: Tell IT/security and follow the approved password-reset guidance.
Use the same password with a different capitalization.
Wait to see if the work account is misused.
Post the password to a team chat so others can check it.

questions.explanation: Credential exposure should be reported and handled using the approved recovery process.

questions.text: What does least privilege mean for employee access?

options.text: Giving everyone administrator access for speed.
Sharing one powerful account across a team.
Having only the access needed for the current work role.
Keeping access forever after a role change.

questions.explanation: Limit permissions to what the job requires and request changes through approval.

questions.text: A caller asks you to read out a one-time authentication code. What should you do?

options.text: Share it if the caller knows your name.
Send it by text instead of saying it aloud.
Refuse and verify the caller independently with IT.
Share half the code to test the caller.

questions.explanation: One-time codes are authentication secrets and should never be disclosed to callers.

questions.text: You typed your password into a page that now looks fake. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the browser and say nothing.
Wait until you see a successful login alert.
Report it quickly and follow the organization's account-recovery instructions.
Change only your personal accounts.

questions.explanation: Do not wait for proof of compromise; responders can advise and check activity.

questions.text: Why should each employee use their own account rather than a shared login?

options.text: It helps the organization know who performed actions and manage access changes.
It prevents all phishing attempts.
It avoids the need for account recovery.
It means permissions never need review.

questions.explanation: Individual accounts support accountability and allow access to change with roles.

questions.text: An attacker learns a password from a shopping site. What makes a work account less exposed?

options.text: The account has no recovery information.
The work account uses a different, unique password.
The password is the same but longer.
The employee shares it only with a manager.

questions.explanation: Unique credentials prevent one service's breach from automatically compromising another account.

questions.text: You are not signing in, but your phone asks you to approve a login. What should you do first?

options.text: Ask a caller to tell you which button to press.
Approve it and check the location afterward.
Disable the phone's notifications.
Deny the prompt; then report it through a known organizational channel.

questions.explanation: Approve only prompts you initiated. Unexpected ones should be rejected and reported.

questions.text: A new team member asks for your account because their access request is taking time. What should you do?

options.text: Create a personal account for them using your email.
Keep your login private and help them use the proper access request.
Give them your MFA device instead.
Share it only while you watch.

questions.explanation: Individual access supports accountability and should be obtained through approved process.

questions.text: You need to create a password for an important work account. Which choice follows the module?

options.text: A strong, unique password stored in the approved manager.
A memorable phrase saved in an unapproved personal note.
The same password used for email and shopping.
A birthday plus the company name.

questions.explanation: Avoid predictable and reused credentials; use approved password management.

questions.text: Your account receives many MFA prompts in a short period. What could this indicate?

options.text: It is a routine reason to turn MFA off.
The app needs you to approve one to synchronize.
The prompts prove the account is safe.
Someone may know your password and is trying to complete sign-in.

questions.explanation: Repeated prompts are suspicious and should be denied and reported.

questions.text: Your role changed and you no longer need access to a finance folder. What is appropriate?

options.text: Explore the folder before access is removed.
Ask the relevant team to remove or adjust the access through the approved process.
Share its contents with your new team.
Keep it in case it is useful later.

questions.explanation: Permissions should reflect current job needs; report or request removal of excess access.

questions.text: A sign-in email contains a link to report an unfamiliar login. What is the safer approach?

options.text: Forward the email to an unknown address.
Reply with your password to confirm ownership.
Click the link because the email mentions your account.
Use the organization's bookmarked site or known reporting route.

questions.explanation: Avoid links in unexpected messages; use a known organizational route.

questions.text: You accidentally approved a sign-in that you did not initiate. What should you do?

options.text: Ask a coworker to log in and check.
Wait to see whether anything changes.
Delete the authentication app.
Report it immediately and follow recovery instructions.

questions.explanation: An unexpected approval may expose the account; prompt reporting supports response.

questions.text: What is an approved password manager meant to help with?

options.text: Sharing a team password with everyone.
Making sign-in alerts unnecessary.
Granting application permissions automatically.
Keeping unique credentials in a safer, organization-approved place.

questions.explanation: A manager helps users handle strong unique credentials without unsafe personal storage.

questions.text: Criminals try a password leaked from one website on a user's work email and file accounts. What is this attack called?

options.text: Credential stuffing
Safe browsing
Screen locking
Data classification

questions.explanation: Credential stuffing uses passwords exposed from one service to try to access other accounts.

questions.text: A single password is reused for email, payroll and a shopping site. What is the main concern?

options.text: The accounts become impossible to recover.
The password manager will reject all accounts.
MFA prompts will stop working.
A breach at one service could help someone access the others.

questions.explanation: Password reuse creates a pathway from one breached account to others.

questions.text: You are distracted and an MFA approval appears unexpectedly. What response protects the account?

options.text: Approve it while distracted and review later.
Reject it rather than approving just to clear the screen.
Turn on automatic approvals.
Send the code to a colleague to decide.

questions.explanation: An approval is a security decision; only accept a sign-in you started.

questions.text: A teammate asks you to log in for them and leave the session open. Why should you decline?

options.text: It might make the screen too bright.
Actions would be tied to your identity and their access would bypass proper controls.
Shared access makes passwords stronger.
The folder would become publicly visible.

questions.explanation: Shared credentials obscure accountability and circumvent the approved access process.

questions.text: Your organization has an approved password manager. Which storage choice should you avoid?

options.text: A supported recovery process.
A unique password for each important account.
The organization's password manager.
A personal notes app not approved for work credentials.

questions.explanation: Unapproved personal storage may not protect work credentials appropriately.

questions.text: An unfamiliar sign-in location appears, but you can still use your account. Should you wait for certainty before reporting?

options.text: No; report the alert promptly and let support assess it.
Yes; only report if work stops.
No; post the alert publicly instead.
Yes; first test whether the location belongs to a colleague.

questions.explanation: Report unusual alerts without trying to prove compromise on your own.

questions.text: You discover your work password matches one exposed in a personal service breach. What now?

options.text: Tell IT/security and follow their reset guidance.
Wait for the next scheduled password change.
Send the old password to IT in an open chat.
Change one letter and use it again.

questions.explanation: Treat possible credential exposure promptly and follow approved recovery guidance.

questions.text: A system offers you broad permissions that your task does not require. What is safest?

options.text: Keep the access after the task ends.
Use a colleague's account instead.
Accept everything because it is available.
